title: Krylov complexity, mode-resolved complexity and entanglement entropy across phase transitions in the non-Hermitian extended Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model
abstract: We investigate phase transitions in the extended Su-Schrieffer-Heeger (SSH) model with next-nearest-neighbor hoppings and an imaginary staggered chemical potential. In the presence of small non-Hermiticity, exceptional points emerge in pairs from the gap-closing momenta near the topological phase boundaries of the Hermitian limit. Utilizing the Krylov spread complexity and entanglement entropy, we analyze two dynamical protocols: (i) preparing the non-Hermitian ground state via a unitary transformation, and (ii) evolving the system under the non-Hermitian Hamiltonian. We show that the spread complexity, and long-time spread complexity as well as entanglement entropy can effectively signal phase transitions in the first and second protocols, respectively. To unravel the detailed structure of the transitions, we introduce the momentum-resolved complexity that identifies the characteristic modes and tracks their evolution with the driving parameter. In the regime where the system possesses a purely imaginary spectrum, we further identify dynamical phases based on the saturation behavior of the spread complexity. The entanglement entropy is also found to exhibit similar saturation behavior, thereby providing a more experimentally accessible probe of the dynamical phases.
summary: The paper analyzes phase transitions in the non-Hermitian extended SSH model using advanced quantum information measures like spread complexity and entanglement entropy. These diagnostics successfully signal topological and dynamical phase changes, even when considering complex spectra. The findings establish these metrics as robust, experimentally accessible probes for understanding non-Hermitian physics.
main_problem: The study investigates how quantum information measures can characterize phase transitions occurring within non-Hermitian extended Su-Schrieffer-Heeger (SSH) models.
main_result: Both spread complexity and entanglement entropy effectively signal the presence of phase transitions, with mode-resolved complexity providing detailed insight into the characteristic modes driving these changes.
method: The authors employ quantum information diagnostics, including Krylov/spread complexity and entanglement entropy, applied to two dynamical protocols: ground state preparation and long-time evolution under non-Hermitian dynamics.
model_or_system: The system is an extended SSH model incorporating next-nearest-neighbor hoppings and an imaginary staggered chemical potential. The Hamiltonian exhibits PT-symmetry and is analyzed in the presence of small non-Hermiticity, leading to exceptional points near topological boundaries.
key_observables: Krylov/Spread complexity ($C$), Mode-resolved complexity, Entanglement entropy ($S$), Saturation times ($	ilde{t}_{EE}^{\epsilon}$), and Exceptional Points (EPs).
important_parameters: Non-Hermiticity strength ($\gamma$), Topological phase boundaries, and the driving parameter controlling the transition.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on mapping complex dynamics onto measurable quantities like complexity and entanglement entropy to detect underlying topological or dynamical phase changes.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate schematic models of the SSH chain, plot spread complexity vs. parameters showing topological boundaries for the Hermitian case, and show distributions of exceptional points in parameter space when non-Hermiticity is introduced.
paper_structure: The paper systematically introduces the non-Hermitian extended SSH model, details the application of complexity measures (Krylov/Spread) and entanglement entropy across two distinct dynamical protocols, analyzes how these diagnostics signal phase transitions near exceptional points, and finally uses mode-resolved analysis to characterize persistent dynamical phases.
why_interesting: This work directly applies advanced quantum information tools (complexity, entanglement) to non-Hermitian topological models, providing a powerful diagnostic framework for characterizing complex many-body dynamics beyond standard spectral methods. This is highly relevant for open quantum systems research.
